opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the analogy is actually pretty misleading, and that's something I've come to feel more strongly about over the years. The way people usually frame it is that a genetic algorithm is a kind of simplified model of evolution: you have a population, you have a fitness function, you select the best, you mutate and recombine, and over time you climb toward some objective. And so the story becomes that evolution is basically an optimizer, and natural selection is pushing everything toward higher fitness.

But when you actually look at what happened in nature, that story doesn't really capture what's interesting about it. Evolution didn't have a target. It wasn't trying to get to humans, or to get to flight, or to get to photosynthesis. There was no objective in the sense that we mean in machine learning. What it really looks like is a massively divergent, open-ended search process that just keeps generating new niches and new ways of living, and each new thing opens up opportunities for other new things. It's more like a prolific generator of novelty than an optimizer.

And the reason this matters is that if you take the conventional genetic algorithm as your model, you end up building systems that converge. They find a solution to the problem you gave them and they stop. That's useful sometimes, but it's the opposite of what made natural evolution remarkable. Nature produced this incredible explosion of diversity in a single run. It never converged. So in a way, the genetic algorithm, as it's typically understood, captures the least interesting part of evolution.

That's a lot of what motivated work like novelty search, where we threw out the objective entirely and just rewarded being different from what came before. And what surprised people was that in some deceptive problems, searching without an objective actually found the solution better than searching for it directly. That tells you something: the stepping stones to great achievements often don't resemble the final achievement. If you're only rewarding things that look like progress toward your goal, you'll miss the stepping stones that actually lead there.

So I'd say the analogy is fine at the level of mechanics: there's variation, there's selection, there's inheritance. But at the level of what the process is *for*, or what it's actually doing, I think it's backwards. Evolution is better understood as an open-ended process, and if we want AI that's truly creative, that keeps inventing things indefinitely, we need to take that seriously rather than treating evolution as just another form of objective optimization.

r001.rationale: The response says the genetic algorithm analogy captures “the least interesting part” of evolution and contrasts it with nature’s open-ended generation of diversity and novelty, arguing that the analogy underestimates evolution’s power.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually a bit of a misleading analogy, and I say that as someone who's spent most of my career working on genetic algorithms and neuroevolution. The problem is that when people hear "genetic algorithm," they picture something very specific: you have a population, you have a fitness function, you select the best individuals according to that function, you mutate and recombine them, and you repeat. That's a search process aimed at an objective. And then people assume that's what evolution in nature is doing, and so they conclude that evolution is basically just a slow, inefficient optimizer, and that gradient descent or whatever else we have is just a better version of the same thing.

But evolution in nature doesn't have an objective in that sense. There's no fitness function sitting out there saying "produce a human" or "produce a bird." Survival and reproduction is a constraint, not a target. And I think that distinction matters enormously, because the thing that's actually remarkable about evolution is not that it optimized anything. It's that it's a divergent process. It produced this astonishing diversity, this constant stream of novelty, photosynthesis, flight, intelligence, all these things that nobody asked for. Nothing was trying to get to them. A conventional genetic algorithm with a single objective is almost the opposite of that. It converges. It collapses the population toward a point.

So when people make that analogy, they end up throwing away the most interesting lesson of evolution, which is that open-ended, non-objective processes can discover things that objective-driven processes can't. That's really what the work on novelty search was about, and what Joel Lehman and I were getting at in the book. If you set an ambitious objective and optimize for it directly, you often get deceived, because the stepping stones to the thing you want don't look like the thing you want. Evolution never had that problem because it wasn't looking for anything in particular.

So I'd say the analogy is fine as a historical note about where the inspiration came from, but it's actually quite harmful if it makes people think of evolution as just another optimizer. The part of evolution that's worth learning from is the part that genetic algorithms, as usually practiced, left out.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the analogy is misleading and harmful because it overlooks evolution’s open-ended capacity to produce novelty that objective-driven genetic algorithms may miss.

astra-6.text:
I think that analogy can be misleading, because what people usually mean by a genetic algorithm is an optimization algorithm. You define a fitness function, you have a population, and you select and reproduce individuals that score well. And then we tend to project that picture back onto evolution, as though evolution were solving a clearly defined problem.

But evolution wasn’t given the objective of producing human intelligence. It didn’t start with bacteria and measure how close they were to becoming humans. There’s no distance-to-humanity function guiding the process. Humans are one of the things that emerged from this enormous, branching process of discovery.

Now, of course, selection matters. Organisms have to survive and reproduce. But what allows them to do that depends on the environment, which includes other organisms that are also evolving. So even the conditions for success are changing as the process unfolds.

To me, the really interesting question is how evolution keeps creating opportunities for further discovery. A conventional genetic algorithm captures some of the mechanics—variation, inheritance, selection—but that doesn’t automatically capture the open-ended creativity. If we equate evolution with optimization too quickly, we risk overlooking precisely the phenomenon we wanted to understand.

r001.rationale: The response says a conventional genetic algorithm captures some mechanics but misses evolution’s open-ended creativity, and warns that equating evolution with optimization overlooks that discovery. This communicates that the equation underestimates evolution’s power.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that analogy can be misleading, because when people hear “genetic algorithm,” they usually imagine that you have some objective function, and evolution is searching for the thing that maximizes it. And then we project that picture onto natural evolution, as though it were trying to produce intelligence, or trying to produce us.

But evolution wasn’t trying to produce us. There wasn’t a fitness function somewhere that said, “Make a human.” There are local pressures to survive and reproduce, but what those pressures mean changes as the world and the organisms in it change. Other organisms are part of your environment, and they’re evolving too.

So selection and mutation are certainly part of the analogy. But if we reduce evolution to optimization toward a fixed goal, we miss this extraordinary capacity to keep generating new possibilities. Intelligence is something that emerged along the way, through stepping stones that weren’t necessarily steps toward intelligence in any obvious sense. That’s the aspect I think we should be paying much more attention to in AI.

r001.rationale: The response says reducing evolution to optimization toward a fixed goal misses its extraordinary capacity to generate new possibilities, arguing that the genetic algorithm analogy understates evolution’s power.
